title: Spider
full_review:
Director David Cronenberg's bleak psychological drama "Spider" (Sony Pictures Classics) burrows into the disturbed mind of a man struggling to discover the truth about his mother's death.

Adapted from the 1990 novel by Patrick McGrath, the film plays with creepy childhood memories, using a technique similar to that seen in "A Beautiful Mind" in which the characters and actions may exist only in the protagonist's mind.

The story is essentially about a disturbed boy who became a disturbed adult, furiously scribbling in his soiled journal, desperate to understand how he got to this state. The deliberate, grinding pace and the film's austere design and narrative approach are reflective of the distorted imagination of Dennis Cleg (Ralph Fiennes). Cleg has just been released after a lifetime of mental institutionalization into a decrepit halfway house painfully close to his East London childhood home, which stirs up many an unsettling memory.

Spider, as Cleg was affectionately called by his mother (Miranda Richardson), takes the viewer back to his adolescence. Flashbacks show a sullen Spider (Bradley Hall), who adores his gentle mother and cowers under the harsh gaze of his plumber father (Gabriel Byrne), whom Spider is frequently sent to fetch from the local pub.

Like the pieces of the jigsaw puzzle Cleg attempts to connect at the halfway house, he pores over his childhood memories, hoping that one section will fit into another and offer him a complete story. At the same time, the viewer is challenged to bring together what actually happened during his gloomy childhood with what the grown man remembers.

Layered into the film is Cleg's intense fear of women that has distorted his outlook and his recollections. Cavorting with his father in the pub are some sassy women, one of whom (at least in Spider's eyes) has the face of his mother. Richardson does triple duty in the film, but in her role as the coarse tart who has caught the wandering eye of Spider's father she is most effective. The viewer cringes as she swigs gin from the bottle or smiles with a mouthful of rotten teeth, carelessly tossing back her peroxide blonde hair.

It seems almost like a rite of passage for actors to play mentally disturbed characters. With very few lines except for an occasional mumble, Fiennes takes a different route than the usual, sympathetic portrayal of the mentally ill. Cleg, with nicotine-stained hands and wearing four shirts at once, is frighteningly out of reach. No connection is made with him, which proves to be a surprisingly effective device in describing the distant and unreachable mind of the mentally ill.

"Spider" is not the sort of well-made film one views for escapist pleasure. Its slow tempo teeters on the tiresome, giving the high-minded narrative a meandering quality. Yet it is appreciably better than most movies made about mentally ill characters because it feels authentic as its grim, barren world reflects a frail, troubled mind.

Due to a few sexual situations, brief violence, and fleeting nudity with a few instances of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
